results.title: 322 | Breaking Analysis | Forecasting the AI bubble: When scarcity turns to surplus - theCUBE Research
highlights:
The bubble bursting does not require AI to fail. It only requires deployable supply and capital commitments to grow faster than monetizable demand. When productive, revenue-producing AI capacity takes longer to materialize, pricing will normalize and financing will no longer bridge the gap. That’s when the capital cycle resets.

But here is the good news for investors.

The AI supply chain remains constrained by high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, network fabric, power and site readiness. These bottlenecks not only slow deployment; they also delay price discovery (i.e., the point at which buyers have more choice), and they postpone the moment when the market discovers whether it has overbuilt.

...

A GPU allocation without sufficient high-bandwidth memory is not deployable capacity. HBM without advanced packaging does not become a working accelerator. Racks require a network fabric to operate as a cluster. And a cluster still requires power, a ready site and capital before it becomes revenue-producing capacity.

The least available layer governs the output of the entire system.

But the key point is that the binding constraint moves. Early in the cycle, the dominant shortage was accelerator availability. It then shifted toward HBM and advanced packaging. As those constraints ease, the pressure moves outward toward networking, power, site readiness and financing. Solving one bottleneck often reveals the next one.

That does two things.

- First, it rations the amount of capacity that can actually reach the market.
- Second, it postpones the market-clearing test – i.e., the moment when we discover how much capacity customers will really consume and what they will pay once supply is broadly available. That’s what we mean by “price discovery.”

...

If memory pricing normalizes while physical bit demand and productive utilization continue to accelerate, that is potentially healthy. The market would be transitioning from a price-led cycle to a volume-led cycle.

But if ASPs fall and bit growth also stalls, that is a more dangerous event. It suggests surplus is arriving faster than useful demand can absorb it.

...

When memory pricing and package lead times normalize together, the bottleneck will likely move downstream. But even then, assembled capacity does not earn a dollar until it reaches a powered site and gets put to productive use.

...

The third scenario is the bubble break.

Here, the scarcity event clears before cash flow catches up. In this scenario, memory and packaging supply expand. Lead times normalize. Memory ASPs and GPU rental prices fall. Backlog conversion slows, productive monetization weakens and customers become less willing to prepay for future capacity. At the same time, debt, equity and third-party financing become less willing to bridge the gap.

Importantly, AI does not have to fail for this scenario to occur. The bubble pops when deployable capacity begins growing faster than profitable utilization – and capital stops financing the difference.

...

Third, watch GPU rental pricing and productive cluster utilization.

Pricing can moderate without being bearish if utilization remains high. Cheaper compute paired with rising consumption could expand the market as the Jevons paradox kicks in. 

The more dangerous combination is rental prices and utilization falling together. That would be the clearest signal that deployable compute supply is beginning to exceed profitable demand.

results.title: [Case Study #40] Is 'Excess GPU' Proof of Overinvestment? — The Secondary Market for Computing Resources Opened by xAI and Meta｜AI革命 20年の羅針盤
highlights:
This time, I will look at the same phenomenon from the supply side. Documents submitted by SpaceX (the company that absorbed the former xAI) to the SEC, and reports based on them, have revealed that only a portion of their AI computing resources (GPUs—specialized chips originally developed for image processing and now used for AI training and inference) are used for their own model, Grok, and the rest are planned to be leased to third parties. Elon Musk himself is also reported to have mentioned this policy. Around the same time, it was reported that Meta is also considering a business to provide its surplus computing resources to external parties. Seeing this, some experts have interpreted it as, 'They bought so much they couldn't use it all, so AI investment was excessive.'

I will state my conclusion first. This case is weak evidence of overinvestment. Rather, it is closer to reality to read it as an early sign of a structural change where a market for lending and borrowing computing resources is about to grow. Judging by the rental prices, what we are seeing is not a fire sale, but demand from external parties with genuine willingness to pay.

However, this is not good news for investors. The fact that the asset known as the GPU is not becoming stranded and continues to hold value in the rental market means that a resolution in the form of a dramatic collapse is not coming. If there is no collapse, there will be no opportunity to buy back at the bottom. What I warned about in the previous issue (#39) was precisely this state of a 'plateau' where 'not even a collapse occurs, and only capital remains dormant.' This observation provides a concrete look from the supply side at the mechanism supporting that plateau.

...

xAI was absorbed into SpaceX in February 2026. The Memphis facility, Colossus 1 (over 220,000 Nvidia chips), built exclusively for Grok, reportedly saw its utilization rate drop to around 10%. This spare capacity became the target for external sales.

It is necessary to carefully distinguish the numbers here. The 'facility scale of Colossus 1 (over 220,000 units)' and the'scale covered by the Anthropic contract' are not the same number. According to documents submitted by SpaceX to the SEC, the contract with Anthropic is worth $1.25 billion per month, runs until May 2029, totals approximately $45 billion, and covers about 325,000 GPUs spanning both Colossus 1 and Colossus 2. In other words, this is more than just moving inventory from one facility; it is a large-scale contract spanning two locations.

The contract with Google is worth $920 million per month, from October 2026 to June 2029, covering approximately 110,000 units including GPUs, CPUs, and memory. Furthermore, in July, it was reported that the AI startup Reflection AI signed a contract to lease the latest chips (GB300) from Colossus 2 for $150 million per month, with a total value of up to $6.3 billion through 2029.

Combining the contracts of the three companies, the total monthly amount is around $2.25 billion. Simply annualized, this is a scale of about $27 billion, which exceeds SpaceX's total company revenue from the previous year. However, this $27 billion is not guaranteed annual revenue. It is necessary to distinguish the following three things as separate entities.

- Monthly contract amount ≠ Annual revenue (will not be realized if canceled)
- Contract period (e.g., until 2029) ≠ Guaranteed operating period (can be terminated with 90 days' notice)
- The fact of signing a contract ≠ The fact that long-term demand is confirmed

...

## 5. Is the price a fire sale or a shortage?

Whether they are 'selling off surplus inventory cheaply' or 'lending scarce items at a high price' can be distinguished by looking at the price. As seen in the previous chapter, the borrower's use is inference, and at least at the time this contract was concluded, there was strong demand there. Let's confirm whether this reading is supported from the price side as well.

When calculating the hourly rate backwards from the disclosed contract amount (calculated as 30.4 days x 24 hours = 730 hours), it is about $11.5 per unit per hour for Google and about $5.3 for Anthropic. However, caution is needed here. This figure is not the price of the GPU alone. The contract includes not only the GPU but a full set of computing resources such as CPU, memory, storage, and high-speed networking, and it is what you might call a 'comprehensive unit price for all computing resources,' divided by the number of GPUs for the total amount. Therefore, this figure cannot be directly compared with the market price of a GPU alone.

With that reservation, it is still worth checking the position of the figures. The cloud rental price for an older generation GPU (H100) alone has fallen to about $2-4 per hour, which is the 'market price for outdated products,' and the spot price in a phase where the latest GPUs (Blackwell series) are tight is said to be about $14 per hour. The two contract unit prices this time (about $5.3-$11.5) are both clearly above this commodity band. What I want to show here is not the argument itself that 'this is expensive.' Since the bundle scope of the contracts is different, the price level itself cannot be directly compared with the market price of a GPU alone. However, it is at a level that is at least inconsistent with the reading that 'surplus equipment that was about to become worthless was disposed of at commodity market prices.' It functions sufficiently as material to show that 'it is not a fire sale'.

...

Google is a company that possesses one of the world's largest amounts of proprietary chips (TPU), and furthermore, the source of the external computing resources is a member of the competing camp (Mr. ... The fact that they went out of their way to borrow a competitor's equipment to secure computing power is material that directly denies the simple supply-excess theory.

...

Capital expenditures related to AI infrastructure are expensed over 5 to 6 years (depreciation). Moreover, because GPU assets become obsolete in terms of performance within a few years, companies find it difficult to choose to 'skip investment this year.' This structure means that even if the revenue obtained from AI does not meet expectations, the expenditures themselves are hard to stop. Even if the demand for computing resources is real, it does not necessarily mean that the suppliers are making sufficient profit. These are two separate questions.

...

There are five indicators to track. The first is whether the unit price rises or falls each time a similar leasing contract is signed in the future. ... The

...

The news that 'idle computing resources are being sold' is not, by itself, proof that AI investment was excessive. What the price tells us is, rather, evidence that there is real demand outside.

The fact that GPUs are idle is not in itself proof of overinvestment. What is important is how much price the idle GPUs command, and whether that price is maintained in six months or a year. If it is equipment whose value becomes zero the moment it is no longer used in-house, a decline in utilization rate is a direct sign of overinvestment. However, if other companies are willing to pay to use them, those GPUs are not 'surplus' but 'assets that can be brought to market.' Therefore, what you should look at is not the GPU utilization rate, but how much price is attached to one hour of idle time.

The fact that GPUs are idle is not proof of overinvestment. Only when the marginal value of idle GPUs begins to disappear should you suspect 'overinvestment.'

And this fact is not material to reassure investors. The fact that assets do not end up stranded also means that the possibility of a resolution in the form of a dramatic collapse is pushed further away.

results.title: Nvidia’s Production Limits Could Slow SpaceX’s Data Center Expansion Next Year – Compute Report
highlights:
Efforts by SpaceX to grow its infrastructure for space-based and terrestrial data centers could slow down due to ongoing component shortages from Nvidia, according to analysts from BNP. The semiconductor company continues to face strong demand that outpaces its manufacturing capabilities, potentially constraining expansion in the cloud computing sector through 2027.

...

While SpaceX pursues its ambitious initiative to deploy data centers in orbit, the company simultaneously develops ground-based facilities designed for similar purposes. These terrestrial infrastructure assets are reportedly in high demand, with third-party companies leasing significant portions of the available capacity. However, analysts highlight that Nvidia, a key provider of essential components such as GPUs that power data center operations, has yet to scale production sufficiently to meet market needs.

The persistent shortfall in Nvidia’s supply chain is not isolated to a single industry but affects a broad range of cloud and AI computing applications. As a result, firms heavily invested in high-performance computing systems, including SpaceX, may find their growth curves limited by the availability of critical hardware.

This bottleneck poses challenges for SpaceX’s vision to revolutionize data processing both on Earth and in space. While the company crafts its space data center blueprint, the ability to install and operate necessary servers depends heavily on having a steady flow of Nvidia components.

As SpaceX’s terrestrial cloud infrastructure rental spaces attract external customers, demand pressure is further intensified. The limited component supplies mean scaling operations to accommodate this demand and future planned expansions will likely be paced slower than originally intended.

Industry observers note that these production constraints could have broader implications for the technology sector’s drive toward greater computational capacity. With Nvidia’s GPUs playing a critical role in AI workloads and cloud computing, the supply imbalance might delay advancements and deployments across multiple verticals.

results.title: IndiaAI Cannot Subsidise Compute and a Sovereign LLM… | AI in Asia
highlights:
On one side sits the compute commons: an ambitious, genuinely novel attempt to make graphics processing units a public utility, rented to Indian startups and researchers at a fraction of hyperscaler prices. On the other sits the sovereign model line, the promise that India will train its own large language models from scratch rather than fine tuning somebody else's weights. Both are defensible. Both are popular. Neither is cheap. And the budget that carries them is smaller than what a single American lab spends on one training run.

...

Now put those numbers against what they are being asked to buy. The compute pillar underwrites a subsidy on empanelled GPU hours. That is a recurring operating expense: every hour a startup burns is an hour the exchequer part pays for, forever, or at least until the subsidy is withdrawn. The foundation models pillar underwrites training runs. That is lumpy capital expenditure with a step function shape, where the difference between a useful model and a frontier competitive one is not twenty per cent more money but an order of magnitude more.

...

Give the compute programme its due, because it has worked better than the sceptics expected. The original target was 10,000 GPUs. By the middle of 2026 the empanelment had passed 38,000 units across fourteen private providers, with roughly fifteen thousand of those in the H100 and H200 class, hosted by operators including Jio, Tata Communications, Yotta and E2E Networks. At the February summit in Delhi, Ashwini Vaishnaw, the electronics and information technology minister, announced a further 20,000 units and set a target of one hundred thousand public GPUs by the end of the year.

The pricing is the genuinely interesting part. The lowest winning bids in the empanelment came in around Rs 116 per GPU hour for standard silicon and Rs 150 per hour for H100 class parts. Eligible users get up to forty per cent off that, and projects deemed to be of national importance can get considerably more. The headline rate quoted from the summit stage was Rs 67 per GPU hour. There is no comparable public offer anywhere in Asia.

But look at the shape of that subsidy. It is a per hour discount with no ceiling on aggregate consumption, funded from a fixed five year envelope. The more successful it is, the faster it exhausts itself. And the money is not fungible in the direction you would want: an hour of subsidised inference for a logistics startup in Pune is an hour that cannot be redirected into a pretraining run.

There is a second, quieter drain. Over eighty five per cent of the subsidy disbursed under the compute pillar has gone not to the broad startup base but to indigenous generative model development. In other words the compute pillar has already been partially annexed by the model pillar. The commons is subsidising the sovereign model programme through the back door, which makes the headline split between the two lines somewhat fictional.

results.title: SpaceX-Nvidia Deal Could Squeeze GPU Supply and Stifle Neoclouds | GFdaily
highlights:
SpaceX has signed a deal with Nvidia for GPUs, a move that could tighten an already strained chip market and put the brakes on the growth of neoclouds—the smaller data-center operators that rent out AI computing power. The agreement, reported in industry circles, comes as demand for high-end accelerators far outstrips supply, and it could reshape the AI infrastructure landscape.

...

Neoclouds are built on the assumption that they can get enough Nvidia chips to serve a booming base of AI startups and researchers. But if SpaceX is pulling a large allocation from the same pool, those operators may find themselves waiting longer for hardware or paying more for what's available. The GPU shortage has already forced some neoclouds to ration capacity or turn away customers. A big new buyer like SpaceX only deepens that squeeze.

...

The deal signals that even the most hardware-hungry players are willing to lock in supply directly with Nvidia, rather than renting from third-party clouds. That could push more enterprises to follow suit, bypassing neoclouds altogether. If that happens, the neocloud business model—essentially a middleman between Nvidia and end users—loses its reason to exist.

...

## The ripple effects on pricing

When a company the size of SpaceX enters the GPU market, it doesn't just buy a few cards. The sheer scale of its order—even if the exact number isn't public—can move prices. GPU rental rates on the spot market have been volatile, and any sign of reduced availability could push them higher. That's a direct hit to neocloud margins, which are already thin because they often sell compute at a discount to win customers.

...

For now, the full terms of the SpaceX-Nvidia deal remain undisclosed. How many GPUs are involved, when they'll be delivered, and whether SpaceX gets priority over other buyers are all open questions. Until those answers come out, neoclouds will be watching their supply forecasts nervously, hoping the rocket company doesn't consume the whole launch pad.

results.title: The GPU Shortage Is Over — But the AI Chip War Is Just Beginning: What's Next for Hardware | Algorithmine
highlights:
Key Takeaways:

- The AI GPU shortage that began in 2022 has officially ended, with lead times normalized and inventory available as of 2026.
- NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture faces intense competition from AMD's MI300 series and Intel's Gaudi 3, creating a true multi-vendor market.
- Hyperscalers like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are accelerating their custom silicon strategies with TPU v5, Trainium2, and Maia chips.
- Total cost of ownership for AI hardware now critically depends on power, cooling, and networking infrastructure, not just chip acquisition.
- Enterprise procurement strategies must evolve to navigate vendor diversification, hybrid cloud models, and complex geopolitical supply chain risks.

...

The GPU shortage that began in late 2022 with the explosive growth of generative AI reached its zenith in 2024. During this period, lead times for NVIDIA's H100 and A100 GPUs stretched to 9-12 months, with some hyperscalers reportedly paying 50-100% premiums on the secondary market. The situation created a two-tier market where only the largest technology companies could reliably procure cutting-edge AI accelerators.

The turning point arrived in mid-2025 as three key factors converged: NVIDIA's production ramp at TSMC's advanced packaging facilities, the maturation of AMD's MI300 production lines, and a temporary cooling in AI investment enthusiasm following the initial generative AI hype cycle. By Q4 2025, lead times had normalized to 8-12 weeks for most enterprise orders, and by Q2 2026, inventory began accumulating at distributors—a stark contrast to the previous three years.

The recovery timeline reveals a critical insight: supply constraints weren't solely about semiconductor fabrication capacity. The bottleneck was in advanced packaging—specifically, TSMC's CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) technology. As TSMC expanded its CoWoS capacity from approximately 120,000 wafers per year in 2023 to over frequent 350,000 by late 2025, the floodgates opened. This packaging capacity expansion, combined with NVIDIA's diversification to multiple OSATs (Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test providers), created the supply elasticity needed to meet demand.

...

### Current Market Status: Inventory, Lead Times, Pricing

As of Q2 2026, the AI accelerator market has entered what industry analysts describe as "supply equilibrium." NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs, once expected to face immediate shortages, are available with lead times of 4-6 weeks for most configurations. AMD's MI300X inventory has normalized to the point where some distributors are offering volume discounts—a phenomenon unthinkable just 12 months prior.

Pricing has followed a predictable but significant downward trajectory. The street price for an NVIDIA H100, which peaked at over $45,000 in late 2024, has settled to approximately $28,000—close to its official list price. More importantly, the secondary market premium has evaporated entirely, with used H100s trading at 60-70% of their original value.

Illustration 2

Inventory levels tell the most telling story. Distributors who previously operated on allocation-only models now maintain 2-4 weeks of inventory for most AI accelerator SKUs. This shift represents a fundamental change in market dynamics—from supplier-controlled scarcity to buyer-influenced competition.
